item.title: A Fight Over Felon Voting Prompts a Free Speech Debate
item.description:
For years, Andrew Cilek and the tiny alliance of election integrity activists he leads have been locked in what he calls “an interpretation battle” over voting rights for felons.

His group, the Minnesota Voters Alliance, believes that the U.S. Constitution forbids voting by felons before the end of their sentences — including parole or probation terms. Minnesota law begs to differ: Since 2023, a criminal record does not affect a citizen’s right to vote in the state unless he or she is incarcerated for a felony conviction.

The disconnect, according to Mr. Cilek, put his group on a collision course with Minnesota’s law prohibiting deceptive practices around elections — part of a surge of rules proposed or passed by states to curb the intentional spread of falsehoods that could suppress the democratic process. Concerned that publicizing its views could trigger the law, Mr. Cilek’s group sued, claiming a First Amendment violation.

The case, Minnesota Voters Alliance, et al. v. Ellison, joins a growing push to govern election-related speech through the judicial system, rather than legislation. A federal appeals court recently ruled in the group’s favor, but Keith Ellison, Minnesota’s attorney general, has vowed to “continue to evaluate next steps.”

The case reflects a time of great confusion and distrust around voting. And with a contentious midterm election just weeks away, it could have major implications for how far states can go to control political expression — what can be articulated at election time, and by whom and where.

The court’s decision conveys to other states that legislating speech is very difficult, said Lawrence R. Jacobs, who runs the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota.

“There’s a near panic among protectors of elections about mis- and disinformation — they consider it to be an epic threat,” he said. “This ruling is a striking example of the limits of what they can do.”

Mr. Cilek, who stressed that he had “a lot” of friends who are felons, said the government viewed his group’s advocacy “as disenfranchisement, but we never intended that — we never even came close to that.”

“We say there’s room for disagreement,” he said. “Reasonable people can disagree on things.”

The case has unfolded in a rapidly changing information environment, especially around elections. Public suspicion and polarization are exacerbated by lax content moderation, distrust in authoritative sources is fanned from the highest political office, and increasingly powerful artificial intelligence technology is undermining faith in reality.

Minnesota has been a hotbed for discussions about the quality of political communications. Local upheaval over federal immigration enforcement policies generated a spate of false narratives and altered visuals last year. Baseless claims of stolen elections dogged the governor’s race this year.

After the 2020 election, when similar voter fraud claims ran rampant, Minnesota was one of several states that tried to address the pollution in the public square by banning voting-related disinformation. Around the country, however, some of that legislation has been dogged by legal challenges, often on First Amendment grounds.

In just one example from last year, the social media platform X sued over a 2023 law that penalized certain election-related deepfakes in Minnesota. (The company claimed “government censorship.”)

Mr. Cilek’s group, founded in 2003 in suburban Roseville, has been involved in multiple cases that have gone before the Minnesota and U.S. Supreme Courts.

Mr. Cilek stresses that his group is officially nonpartisan, but allows that its beliefs can lean conservative. Its ties to conservative donors and legal groups have helped fuel its many lawsuits over voting practices in Minnesota — such as in 2023, when it sued after state lawmakers restored voting rights to felons who were not incarcerated.

One lawmaker, a Democrat, described that lawsuit as an attempt “to create confusion and fear.” In 2024, the Minnesota Supreme Court dismissed the case on standing.

The group also took issue with the state’s deceptive-practices law, which was passed in 2023. The law threatens misdemeanor charges and a fine of up to $1,000 against those who knowingly transmit falsehoods that could impede voting within 60 days of an election. Lawmakers hoped to prevent lies about logistics and eligibility that could suppress voting by Black citizens and others.

But Mr. Cilek’s group felt that its public advocacy on felon voting rules put a target on its back and could expose it to prosecution. Mr. Cilek wrote opinion pieces arguing against early re-enfranchisement, among other efforts. So the group sued again, pre-emptively, claiming that the deceptive-practices law enabled government retaliation against unsanctioned ideas.

Government officials filed a counterclaim, accusing the alliance of making intimidating statements that it knew were “materially false under Minnesota law.” State Representative Emma Greenman, the chief author of the deceptive-practices rule, said in an interview that the voters group and its allies were perpetuating “a cottage industry of challenging our voter protection laws”

“This is part of a strategy of moving the policy preferences and decisions out of the democratically elected legislatures and Congress and into the courts,” said Ms. Greenman, a Democrat and, for two decades, a voting rights lawyer. “At the end of the day, whether the intent is there or not, it weakens people’s relationship to their power and our democracy.”

The courts have delivered mixed decisions.

A federal judge first dismissed the Minnesota Voters Alliance’s case in the fall of 2024. Nearly two years later, in August, a panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit decided in the alliance’s favor, ruling that the group’s views qualified as protected political speech

Minnesota’s law cut off “open and vigorous expression of views” and could be abused by running out the clock until after the election, the judges wrote. Instead, the panel added, state officials could push back against false speech by publicly countering it with facts, and even informing parolees and probationers directly about their rights.

The ruling bars Minnesota officials from trying to block the advocacy group’s speech related to felon voting rights. This month, the full Eighth Circuit court rejected the state’s petition for a rehearing. The state attorney general’s office said in a statement that it would keep trying “to defend the constitutionality” of the law. On Tuesday, Mr. Ellison, the attorney general, introduced a form that Minnesotans could use to report incidents of disinformation or deceptive technology related to the midterms, including A.I.-generated deepfakes.

In the past, free speech cases have sometimes been resolved, even as high as the U.S. Supreme Court, in favor of calculated falsehoods, said Ciara Torres-Spelliscy, a law professor specializing in election law and the First Amendment at Stetson University’s College of Law.

“My fear, given the way they’ve ruled in past cases, is that they are going to side with the people who are producing disinformation in elections at the expense of American voters,” she said.

All of this is giving Mr. Cilek déjà vu. In 2010, he went to his polling place on Election Day wearing a button calling for photo ID requirements for voters and a T-shirt with a logo for the conservative Tea Party movement. He was temporarily prevented from voting.

The experience turned into Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky. The case considered whether Minnesota’s law banning apparel with political messaging at active polling stations violated the First Amendment.

“I was hoping the case would go away because I hated it,” Mr. Cilek said. “I mean, it’s a T-shirt. I didn’t realize the magnitude of it.” The U.S. Supreme Court heard the case in February 2018 and voted 7 to 2 in the alliance’s favor.

Today, embroiled in another free speech case, Mr. Cilek, 62, said he had no interest in spending more time publicizing his group’s position on felon voting rights. He’s tired, and his priorities have shifted, he said last month during an interview at a mall food court in the Minneapolis suburb where he lives.

Still, Mr. Cilek said, he wouldn’t mind having another go at the Supreme Court.

“That’d be fun to just go there one more time, except this time I’d have a little more experience,” he said.

For Representative Greenman, the fight against election interference is far from over. Her own law was narrowly conceived, she said, meant to target a specific kind of deception historically used around elections.

”The much harder work involves the general disinformation that is coming from the president of the United States and then being recycled and passed on,” she said. “This isn’t going to help us, in the age of A.I. and technology, with some of the much more aggressive and prevalent falsehoods that are being spread, and spread rapidly.”

item.title: Attention, Passengers: High Airfares May Be Here to Stay
item.description:
Airfares soared because of the war with Iran. It’s looking increasingly likely that prices won’t come down anytime soon.

Tensions in the Middle East have risen in recent days, pushing up oil prices. But even if the war ended and fuel costs fell, ticket prices could remain stubbornly high.

Travelers, particularly affluent ones who buy high-end seats, have been undeterred so far by the higher prices. Other costs for the airlines are up. And they are facing less competition. Spirit Airlines, which once offered tickets for less than $100, shut down this spring, and other low-cost carriers are struggling.

“It’s expensive to fly airplanes,” Scott Kirby, the chief executive of United Airlines, told Wall Street analysts in a conference call on Wednesday. Most companies in his industry will lose money this year, so fares will have to remain high, he said. “I think the tide has to rise for everyone or those airlines simply won’t exist.”

In September, airfares were 22 percent more expensive than a year earlier, according to federal data. The average cost of a round-trip Thanksgiving flight within the United States is currently about $389, about 39 percent more than it was at this time last year, according to Hopper, a booking app known for its price-tracking features. Similar flights for Christmas are averaging $452, up 22 percent from a year ago.

Fuel typically accounts for about 25 to 30 percent of an airline’s operating costs, behind only wages and employee benefits. So when jet fuel prices nearly doubled in March, airlines raised fares. Jet fuel prices fell in the spring, but have steadily climbed since July. Today, they are about as high as they have been since the United States and Israel began attacking Iran on Feb. 28.

American Airlines and United each said this past week that their fuel costs in the quarter that ended in September were nearly $1.9 billion higher than the same period last year. United said it had recaptured 72 percent of that cost, though it expected to recover the rest eventually.

Other expenses have increased, too. Landing fees and airport rents were up 9 to 14 percent in the third quarter from a year earlier for several airlines.

Airlines are also paying employees more after negotiating new labor contracts with pilots, flight attendants and other workers in recent years. American, Delta Air Lines and United each spent 7 to 10 percent more on salaries, wages and benefits during the first nine months of this year than they did in the same period in 2025.

Airline executives say ticket price increases are long overdue to cover such costs. Adjusted for inflation, the average fare for a flight within the United States last year was 25 percent cheaper than a decade ago, according to federal data, which does not include fees.

In the past, travelers could expect fares to come down once fuel prices fell. As costs dipped, airlines would have cut prices to win over as many customers as possible.

But the industry is changing. Carriers are less concerned with filling planes and more so with attracting customers who will pay for more comfortable seats and better service.

That is, in part, because budget carriers are no longer the powerhouses they once were. A little over a decade ago, Spirit had some of the industry’s highest profit margins. But Spirit shut down in May, after struggling with high costs and competition, notably from larger airlines that offered no-frills “basic economy” tickets to lure customers from Spirit and other low-cost carriers. The airline’s demise already appears to have contributed to higher fares in some places.

Southwest Airlines, which also had a reputation for bringing down prices, is remaking itself in the mold of American, Delta and United by charging bag fees and removing seats from its Boeing 737 planes to make space for more expensive ones with extra legroom.

Delta and United are by far the most profitable airlines today because they have focused on selling premium seats and keeping customers loyal by offering big spenders generous perks. The sale of economy cabin seats — once the bread-and-butter of airlines — now accounts for less than half of Delta’s revenue. American has said leisure travelers are buying nearly two-thirds of the airline’s premium and business-class seats.

John Dalton is one of the customers airlines covet. Mr. Dalton, an actor who teaches theater appreciation to older people in Miami, has always loved to travel. He first bought a business-class ticket a decade ago for a trip to Europe to celebrate overcoming cancer. Today, he tries to fly business on most long trips, even if it means reducing other spending.

“I was like, ‘OK, I’ll splurge on getting a business class seat,’ and then I liked it, which was the curse,” he said. “All of a sudden, you’re like, ‘Oh, this is the way it could be,’ to the point that I dread having to fly coach.”

Generally, customers have accepted double-digit fare increases with a “limited amount of resistance,” Delta’s chief executive, Ed Bastian, said on an earnings call this month.

And while budget travelers have pulled back a bit, some airline executives said they were not too anxious about losing a few customers. American, Alaska Airlines and United recently said they were flying slightly emptier planes while collecting much more revenue. That is “a trade we would make every day,” United’s chief commercial officer, Andrew Nocella, said on the earnings call.

The question now is whether airlines will be able to resist the urge to lower prices to fill those seats.

Some industry experts said airline executives were using their public statements, especially their conference calls with analysts, to signal to investors and one another that they did not plan to lower fares.

“They will willingly discount-shame anybody who has the temerity to try to break price,” said Robert Mann, an industry consultant and former airline executive.

Mr. Mann said there are fewer airlines in the United States than in the past, which means the remaining companies may feel less pressure to lower fares.

Airlines cycle between flooding the market with seats and retrenching. In 2024, carriers were optimistic about demand and significantly increased the number of flights they offered during the summer. The resulting glut of seats forced companies like Spirit to cut prices. That contributed to Spirit’s downfall, which has reduced the number of seats for sale, thus easing the pressure on airlines to lower fares.

Over a longer stretch of time, the balance could again swing back in the favor of travelers.

This month, Boeing received long-delayed federal approval to start delivering the largest version of its 737 Max plane. United and Alaska are expected to receive 19 and 22 of those planes next year. Southwest also expects to start receiving the smallest Max variant, which was certified in August.

And if the economy weakens and stocks fall sharply, many affluent travelers may rethink their spending on travel, opting for fewer trips, downgrading to economy seats or shopping around for lower fares.

Even travelers like Mr. Dalton have their limits. As major airlines start offering “basic business” fares that strip away perks like lounge access or extra checked bags, he is becoming more willing to shop around.

“It makes me feel less loyal to an airline,” he said, “if they’re nickel-and-diming everything.”

item.title: Noah Adams, Longtime Host of ‘All Things Considered,’ Has Died at 84
item.description:
Noah Adams, a longtime host of NPR’s “All Things Considered” whose quiet baritone and empathetic ear brought listeners stories of back-roads America not often heard on the national airwaves, died on Oct. 16 at his home in Yellow Springs, Ohio. He was 84.

The cause was complications of a benign brain tumor removed eight years ago, his wife, Neenah Ellis, said.

Mr. Adams was a postman’s son from Kentucky who never finished college, and he worked hard to lose the Appalachian accent that he knew conjured up negative stereotypes about his native region.

But he never lost his respect for rural and working-class Americans, and he delighted in leaving Washington, where NPR is based, to travel around the country interviewing miners, farmers, single mothers and factory workers.

In the morning meetings, where the day’s events and newsmakers were discussed, Ms. Ellis, who worked in production at NPR, recalled, “He was looking for who was yearning, who was in pain, who needed help out in the country.”

Mr. Adams abhorred interviewing officials with pat talking points, though that was often part of his job as host of the weeknight edition of “All Things Considered,” NPR’s flagship news and interview show, a position he held for 18 years. He preferred to seek out regular people whose lives were affected by national events.

“The best stories come from west of the Potomac,” he once said.

His respect for his sources came through in interviews of those unaccustomed to a microphone.

“He was wonderfully warm and conversational with people,” said Melissa Block, another host of “All Things Considered,” who worked as a producer for Mr. Adams early in her career. “I don’t know that anyone talking with him would think, ‘Oh, the interview is about to start.’ It would just be a conversation.”

From 1982 to 1987, Mr. Adams’s co-host on “All Things Considered” was Susan Stamberg, an emotive, brainy New Yorker. It was a matchup that showed how opposites attract.

“He is the most genuine, uncontrived voice in broadcasting,” Ms. Stamberg wrote in the introduction to a 1992 book that Mr. Adams wrote about a year of his work for NPR.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

After a short hiatus, he returned to host “All Things Considered” with Robert Siegel and Linda Wertheimer from 1989 until 2002.

“He was a very private and shy person,” Mr. Siegel said in an interview.

After Mr. Adams wrote a book about learning to play the piano at 51, “Piano Lessons” (1997), Mr. Siegel recalled Mr. Adams’s distress at realizing that he would have to perform on his book tour: “I watched him at a Borders, and he was terrified. But he loved what he did. He pulled it off very beautifully.”

During his time away from NPR, from 1987 to 1989, Mr. Adams was recruited to host a replacement show for the much-loved “A Prairie Home Companion,” whose creator, Garrison Keillor, had left. The replacement, “Good Evening,” was another folksy variety show broadcast live from a theater in St. Paul, Minn. It was enlivened by Mr. Adams’s essays about the community on the St. Croix River where he had settled, but it struggled to replicate Mr. Keillor’s audience.

The show lasted less than a year, and Mr. Adams announced his departure shortly before it ended. “I never felt people were saying, ‘Gee, that’s not Garrison Keillor,’” he later said somewhat defensively.

Noah Donald Adams was born on Sept. 15, 1942, in Ashland, Ky., the elder of fraternal twin boys. His father, Roy Adams, and his mother, Edith (Wellman) Adams, a secretary, divorced soon after, and Noah and his brother, James, were raised by their mother and maternal grandparents.

Noah graduated from Ashland High School (now Paul G. Blazer High School) and attended Eastern Kentucky State College (now Eastern Kentucky University) for 18 months before being asked to leave because he was living in unauthorized off-campus housing and writing term papers for football players.

He knocked around doing various jobs, — including construction and car sales, before joining the University of Kentucky’s public radio station, WBKY (now WUKY), in Lexington. There, he hosted a progressive rock show and worked the control board for other shows.

After writing a letter to NPR, he was hired in 1975 as a production assistant on “All Things Considered,” which had been introduced four years earlier. In 1978, he became a weekend co-host for the show.

A 90-minute documentary that he co-wrote about the mass suicide at Jonestown in Guyana in 1978, “Father Cares: The Last of Jonestown” (1981), received wide notice for its innovative format and subject. It was based on 900 hours of recordings that the cult leader Jim Jones and his followers had made before their deaths. Mr. Jones’s voice was so chilling, The Minneapolis Star Tribune noted, that “a listener might cling to the rational tone of narrator Noah Adams as to the hand of a friend.”

Though he preferred feature reporting, Mr. Adams did not shy away from hard news at home or abroad. He won an award from the Overseas Press Club of America in 1994 for work he did in Serbia on the roots of the country’s national extremism.

On Sept. 11, 2001, he was on the air from the morning until after dark, updating millions of listeners about the terrorist attacks. He called it the most important day of his career, when he could “feel the audience” intent on understanding the shocking events, Ms. Ellis said.

The following year, Mr. Adams took a leave of absence to research a book about the Wright brothers, one of five nonfiction books he wrote. When he returned, it was as a contributing correspondent on NPR’s national desk. He roamed widely but regularly returned to stories in Appalachia.

Ms. Ellis, who married Mr. Adams in 1987, recalled visiting Appalachia for the first time with him. They were on assignment — she was his producer — and he instructed her and an engineer on how to approach strangers wary of outsiders. You don’t knock on their doors, he told them: “You drive up, get out of the car and stand there until they come out.”

Mr. Adams’s first two marriages ended in divorce. In addition to Ms. Ellis, he is survived by his brother.

Among the thousands of stories that Mr. Adams reported, the one that got the most enthusiastic response was when he visited a New York recording studio and sang a wobbly version of the Eagles song “Take It to the Limit.”

He played the tape on the air for Ms. Stamberg, who squealed, “It’s adorable!”

One of the hundreds of listeners who wrote in said, “I was getting ready to drop out of law school and we were thinking about getting a divorce, but if you have the courage to stand in that studio and play it for Susan on the radio, then I know we can do anything we really set our minds to.”

item.title: Caryle Murphy Has Died. She Earned a Pulitzer for Reporting in Kuwait.
item.description:
Caryle Murphy, whose intense, monthlong coverage of Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait in 1990 for The Washington Post — an assignment that ended with her escape to Saudi Arabia from Saddam Hussein’s forces — earned her a Pulitzer Prize, died on Oct. 19 in Fairfax County, Va. She was 79.

Her death, in a hospital, was caused by viral pneumonia, her husband, Herbert Howe, said. In 2015, Ms. Murphy had been diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis and three years later received a lung transplant.

Ms. Murphy was The Post’s bureau chief in Cairo in late July 1990, when David Ignatius, the paper’s foreign editor, called to tell her there was reliable information that the Iraqis were likely to invade. At the time, she had a mysterious ailment that left her struggling to stay awake.

“I said, ‘Can you possibly get to Kuwait?’” Mr. Ignatius recalled in an interview. “She got off her sickbed and was one of the few correspondents from American journalism in Kuwait when the tanks rolled in.”

Over four weeks, she reported from Kuwait City about roads littered with burned-out armored cars and trucks; early signs of Kuwaiti resistance; embassies that were under siege; the absence of civil administration; and antiwar protests, mostly by women.

“When someone takes your country,” a Kuwaiti woman told Ms. Murphy, “it’s like tearing out your heart.”

Ms. Murphy felt she was in danger of being rounded up by Iraqi forces and left her hotel to hide in homes, first with Americans and then with Kuwaitis. With phone and Telex lines dead, she had to find other means to send her stories, which included passing them to people leaving Kuwait or rolling them into a tube, with a note identifying herself, and tossing them over the wall of a friendly embassy. The U.S. embassy would not let her use its classified communications channels.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

Some of her stories carried her byline but, after a few days, The Post removed her name to protect her.

She decided to leave Kuwait for several reasons, including not wanting to subject the family that was hiding her to Iraqi threats to hang anyone sheltering a Westerner. One attempt to flee failed. But on Aug. 27, wearing a black veil and robe, she escaped from Kuwait in a nine-vehicle caravan that drove four hours across the desert to Saudi Arabia.

“Stranded cars, left by their occupants, litter the landscape,” she wrote in The Post. “No one talks as our car bounces over the sandy ridges. Three times, we have to stop to dig out one of the vehicles. Two are finally abandoned because their engines died. We meet only two Iraqi soldiers, but they don’t attempt to stop us.”

She remained largely in Saudi Arabia, where in January and February 1991 she covered the Persian Gulf war, in which a military coalition led by the United States liberated Kuwait.

A few months later, she was awarded the Pulitzer for international reporting, which she shared with Serge Schmemann of The New York Times for his coverage of the reunification of Germany.

“It’s really nice to get the mother of all prizes,” Ms. Murphy told The Post newsroom. She also won the George Polk Award for foreign reporting.

Carole Marie Murphy — who change the spelling of her first name in the 1960s to make it more distinctive — was born in Hartford, Conn., on Nov. 16, 1946, and grew up in Brockton, Mass. Her father, Thomas, was a pediatrician, and her mother, Muriel (McCarthy) Murphy, managed the home while raising six children.

In 1968, Ms. Murphy earned a bachelor’s degree in history from Trinity College in Washington (now Trinity Washington University); years later, in 1986, she received a master’s degree in international public policy from the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies.

Looking to travel after her undergraduate degree, she taught English and history for two years at an all-girls’s school in Nyeri, Kenya. Back in the United States, she started her journalism career at The Brockton Enterprise before going back overseas as a freelancer.

In 1976, she was reporting for The Post from Angola — one year after the African country became independent from Portugal but during its civil war — when she was accused by the government of working for the C.I.A. She was placed under house arrest for more than a week, interrogated over her sources for one article and expelled from the country.

She was soon hired full-time by The Post, starting as a suburban reporter in Virginia before being assigned to South Africa from 1977 to 1982. She then returned to cover immigration and other beats.

In 1984, she met Robert Gersony, a consultant to the State Department who told her about mass killings of civilians in Uganda under the strongman leader Milton Obote.

Mr. Gersony had gained no traction within the Reagan administration to intervene to stop the killings, which, she wrote in The Post, were considered by Ugandans and foreign observers “worse than the atrocity-ridden eight-year rule of the country’s former ruler, President Idi Amin.”

The publicity generated by Ms. Murphy’s article “stopped the killings,” Mr. Gersony said in an interview, in part by leading Elliott Abrams, the assistant secretary of state for human rights, to tell the BBC at the time that Uganda no longer had the backing of the United States. The interview was heard around Africa, and Mr. Obote soon met with Chester A. Crocker, the assistant secretary of state for African affairs.

In response to the exposure of the killings, Mr. Gersony recalled, the Obote government opened the Luwero Triangle — the region where the International Committee of the Red Cross estimated that more than 300,000 people were killed — to relief operations.

“The government delegitimized itself with its actions,” Mr. Gersony said. “And Caryle’s article was the vehicle for breaking the Obote government,” which fell in a bloodless military coup in 1985.

Ms. Murphy joined The Post’s Cairo bureau in 1989 and reported from the Middle East for five more years, before moving to the religion beat. After taking a buyout from the paper in 2006, she returned to Saudi Arabia two years later as a freelancer for The Christian Science Monitor and other publications.

As a public policy scholar at the Wilson Center, she researched and wrote “A Kingdom’s Future: Saudi Arabia Through the Eyes of Its Twentysomethings” (2013). It was her second book, following “Passion for Islam: Shaping the Modern Middle East: The Egyptian Experience” (2002). She also wrote about religion for the Pew Research Center.

In addition to her husband, whom she married in 2017, Ms. Murphy is survived by two sisters, Karen Burke and Colleen Kirchgessner; and two brothers, Kevin and Kenan Murphy.

In one of her final dispatches from Kuwait, in August 1990, Ms. Murphy wrote in a first-person story that a week before the Iraqi invasion, Mr. Hussein’s “bullying rhetoric and even his huge military buildup on the border, still seemed like distant, familiar rumbles to most Kuwaitis.

“Invasion? ‘Forget it,’ they said. ‘We’ve heard all this before from Iraq.’”

Everything still seemed normal, she wrote. The city’s beaches were crowded, and the Kuwaiti military had not been placed on alert, for fear that Mr. Hussein would be provoked.

“It was,” she wrote, “a fatal mistake.”

item.title: Why Some People Are Paying to Make Friends
item.description:
Last year, Alexandra Pitzer paid $290 to meet a group of strangers.

Ms. Pitzer, 33, had just relocated from Nashville to Honolulu for her husband’s Army job when an Instagram ad for a friendship matching app caught her attention. The app, Real Roots, organizes get-togethers for groups of women after they fill out a personality survey. If the women get along, they can pay Real Roots to arrange meet-ups with the same group for the next several weeks.

Ms. Pitzer clicked in, signed up and soon found herself at a brewery with eight other women. They quickly bonded, and she continued meeting some of them after the package ended, going camping and to the beach.

“I can see most of them being lifelong friends,” Ms. Pitzer said. “We have a genuine connection.”

Fueled by a loneliness epidemic and increasingly online lifestyles, more people are paying start-ups to make new friends offline. And friend-matching companies such as Real Roots, 222 and Timeleft are exploding in popularity as a result, each one generating millions of dollars in revenue annually.

The start-ups are meant to remove the strain caused by online dating and other meet-up apps — no profiles to swipe through, no schedules to align, no locations to discuss.

When they sign up, the apps’ tens of thousands of users, typically in their 20s to their 50s, fill out questions related to their background, interests and values. The companies consider unusual criteria like sense of humor, how you like to spend time with friends and if you like meeting people on the other side of the political spectrum.

Once users pick an event off the apps’ calendars, the companies’ algorithms kick into motion. Users are matched with a small group from all the people who signed up — based on characteristics like age and other answers — and told to meet at a predetermined location.

Sometimes it’s a designated table at a restaurant. Other times it’s a bus to a hike, a dumpling-making class or shuffleboard. Once they have paid, all they have to do is show up.

“I think our generation craves the in-real-life environment of meeting each other in a more intimate setting, without digital preconceptions,” said Arman Roshannai, one of 222’s co-founders.

The concept of connecting strangers in person has proved successful, and more start-ups have entered the market. In September, Tinder, the dating app, started a “Group Hangout” feature to help friends plan “in-real-life activities together.”

The apps are taking off at a time when about 67 percent of adults have reported social-emotional loneliness, in part because they did not feel part of a meaningful group, according to a 2024 study by the Making Care Common Project at Harvard University. About 45 percent of lonely adults said they “don’t really know how to develop close friendships.”

“I think it’s a fragile time in the world, and a lot of young people are also feeling vulnerable in a variety of ways,” said Richard Weissbourd, a psychologist and senior lecturer at Harvard and co-author of the report.

In August, 25-year-old Sylvia Le paid around $170 to attend a mountain day-trip organized by 222. Ms. Le, who works in marketing, moved to New York in April after growing up on the West Coast.

The day of the event, she went to a meeting point at Washington Square Park, after which she rode on a bus with her assigned group for an hour and a half. They hiked and had lunch before heading back into the city.

“It can kind of feel kind of awkward for me, sometimes, to socialize when that’s the whole point of the dinner, or something like that,” she said. “So having the activity just makes it more natural.”

That type of human connection was the reason Mr. Roshannai, Keyan Kazemian and Danial Hashemi came up with 222 as part of a research project in college to “crack the code on human compatibility.”

A year after the country had shut down during the pandemic, the students received a $1,000 grant from University of California, Irvine, to study whether personality survey data could help predict social compatibility. They got their friends to fill out surveys, then expanded the effort by recruiting other students.

After first connecting groups over video calls, the 222 founders started hosting dinners in their backyard. The project became a full-time job in 2023.

Since then, 222, which employs 27 people, has expanded into 21 cities and hosts at least one experience a day. The app asks potential matches questions like “What do you think about astrology?” and “How attractive do you consider yourself?” It charges $22 a month to match people and curate the event, on top of costs that may be associated with experience, like the fees for a yoga class or the meal paid for a dinner.

The company tripled revenue last year and is on track to quadruple revenue this year to the high seven figures, according to the co-founders.

Real Roots and Timeleft have experienced similar demand. Real Roots got its start when a co-founder, Dorothy Li, was looking to make friends after moving to San Francisco and hosted group hangouts in her apartment with women she met online. She decided to build the experience into an app, which was introduced in 2024. Real Roots, which arranges activities for groups of women from bowling to scavenger hunts, is in 120 cities.

Timeleft started a similar app to coordinate dinners with strangers in 2023, after several prior iterations failed, the start-up’s founder, Max Barbier, said. The app is now available in more than 200 cities.

The apps are not always a hit. Some users complain on social media that they did not click with their group or that the experiences can feel awkward and forced.

Alex Cheney, 34, attended several friendship-matching events in cities including Los Angeles — organized by apps like Timeleft, Groupvibe and Kin — over the last two years. But he did not form any meaningful friendships, he said.

“In terms of building a deep friendship, it’s almost something that you have to explore and co-create and build in real time,” said Mr. Cheney, who had also tried building a matching algorithm for coffee meet-ups. “I don’t necessarily know if it’s something that you can build into a matching algorithm because you might have a lot of compatibility on paper with someone.”

For others, it has proved more successful.

Lauren Valenti, an executive assistant in finance, tried a Real Roots meet-up in San Francisco in February. Ms. Valenti, 38, was single at the time and lived alone, while many of her friends had families. She realized she was stuck in a trap of dating for social connection.

At her first meet-up at a wine bar, she connected with two other women who were similarly the single friends in their friend groups. They felt so comfortable, they even talked about personal topics like freezing their eggs.

“It felt so good to finally see someone equal to myself and share that connection,” she said. She paid roughly $290 for the package and committed to a six-week-long series of meet-ups.

Today, she has a group chat with her friends from her first meet-up and sees them regularly. They also reach out to one another for advice.

“There’s one girl that I’m about to message and be like, ‘Hey, girl, I have a ton of clothes I’m trying to get rid of in my closet — they’re all yours if they want them,” Ms. Valenti said.

item.title: A Song in Your Heart and a Pillow Under Your Head: 5 Hotels for Music Lovers
item.description:
Music lovers have long been willing to travel to see their favorite acts, and in turn hotels have played up their proximity to concert venues. These days, more hotels are striving to become music destinations in their own right. Some are themed, like Dolly Parton’s new SongTeller Hotel in Nashville, Tenn. Others are providing instrument lessons, listening rooms, recording studios, D.J. residencies and on-site concert series, be it at design hotels (like the Parker Palm Springs, which this month began offering Parker Sessions in a new amphitheater) or at major chains such as W, Virgin, Hard Rock and Sonesta International.

Below are some of the latest spots where music is at the heart of the hotel’s character. Whether you’re interested in rock, jazz, blues or electronic music, these getaways aim to put a song in your heart and a pillow under your head.

San Antonio, Texas

This over-100-year-old hotel in downtown San Antonio — where in 1936 the blues musician Robert Johnson made one of his rare recordings — has reopened after a $70 million renovation. Big band musicians, including Alphonse Trent, Mack Rogers and Henry Lange, once led the in-house orchestras, and while the Beaux-Arts-influenced hotel has been updated with reimagined spaces and new dining concepts (it also joined Marriott’s Tribute Portfolio), its musical ties remain. All of its 311 rooms and suites have record players, along with a copy of a Johnson album. A vinyl library with more than 1,000 records allows you to check out your favorite.

Regular performances, be it mariachi or country music, are part of the experience. On Wednesdays, stop by the new Studio Lounge Sessions music series, where a lead artist typically invites friends to make music together. Bar 414 (named for the room number where Johnson recorded) offers free live music (the schedule is here). And the Crystal Ballroom has ticketed concerts on special occasions.

From Nov. 12 to 14, there will be a celebration of the 90th anniversary of the Johnson recordings featuring his grandson, Steven Johnson, and performances by artists, including the pedal-steel guitarist Robert Randolph. Ally Venable, Tomar & the FCs and Nicky Diamonds will also perform, and there will be tours of the hotel’s new recording studio.

In addition to Bar 414, you’ll find three other places to grab a bite. Prices from $250 a night; see the website for packages and offers.

Wanship, Utah

When the luxury hospitality group Auberge Collection began noticing traveler interest in music tourism, it created its own concert series, featuring performances in intimate settings. At the Lodge at Blue Sky, a 46-room-and-suite getaway set on a 4,000-acre private ranch in the Wasatch Mountain Range, about half an hour from Park City, upcoming performances include HARDY (Nov. 21) and Maren Morris (Dec. 4).

In addition to attending concerts in what was once the property’s indoor riding arena, you can go hiking, mountain biking, horseback riding, snowshoeing or try a massage, yoga or guided meditation. Yuta, the main restaurant, serves regional cuisine, including Utah rib-eye and lamb rack, and organic produce from the lodge’s farm.

Accommodations have picturesque views and include suites, many with outdoor fireplaces. Room prices are from $1,800 a night. Packages and à la carte concert ticket options and prices vary by artist. The Auberge Concert Series schedule, including seat details and pricing, is at Auberge.com/music.

New York

This 201-room-and-suite hotel in Midtown Manhattan is home to a new 1940s-and-’50s-inspired jazz club with 170 seats. Known as the Pocket, the club is a nod to the jazz rooms that populated 52nd Street in that era. On any given night, amid the green leather banquettes, cherry wood and the 1964 Steinway grand piano, you might hear jazz, Latin music, hip-hop, R&B or soul.

Musicians scheduled to perform in November include Grammy Award winners such as Mingus Big Band, Arturo O’Farrill & the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra, and the New Orleans-based Dirty Dozen Brass Band. Complement the music with a martini or an Old Fashioned, and order from a menu that includes starters like broiled oysters in various styles; entrees such as prime rib, roasted chicken, fish or “broccoli steak”; and for dessert, pies from the Four & Twenty Blackbirds bakery, including salted caramel apple crumb and rhubarb crumble.

After the show, retire to your graphic black-and-white room (some rooms have outdoor space). Prices from $299 a night. For the latest performance schedule and ticket information visit thepocketnyc.com/calendar.

Madrid; London; Tulum, Mexico

UMusic Hotels are a remix of traditional hotels, places to both sleep and enjoy live events. In December, UMusic Hotel Denmark Street is scheduled to open in London’s Soho neighborhood, named for the street that’s long been associated with the British music business and musicians like Elton John and the Sex Pistols. The Lower Third, a live music venue (and the name of a band David Bowie once worked with), is on Denmark Street, while the 2,000-seat music and performance venue, Outernet Live, is close by. The new 26-room-and-suite hotel will include a lobby cocktail bar and a fitness room, and will sit in the midst of the action.

Also in December, the brand plans to open UMusic Hotel & Beach Club Tulum, with 57 rooms and villas (some with Jacuzzis or private pools) and a beach club. The property is being designed as a destination for live music and other events, and will have recording studios and production facilities as well as beach access and a pool.

UMusic Hotels is developing properties in Kansas City and Austin as well, but in the meantime you can check out the first of its hotels, UMusic Hotel Madrid, which is near Plaza Mayor and has 130 rooms and suites, and access to the Teatro Albéniz from the hotel lobby. The hotel also has a vinyl library and a piano bar. Prices from €350 a night.

Paris

In 1965, a nightclub called Bus Palladium opened in the capital’s Pigalle district, attracting revelers like Serge Gainsbourg, David Bowie and the Rolling Stones. Today, that nightclub has been reimagined as a five-story boutique hotel with a subterranean club where Madonna and Charli XCX have performed.

Designed by Karl Fournier and Olivier Marty, co-founders of the Paris-based architecture firm Studio KO, the hotel has 35 rooms and suites that mix elements of Brutalism, like raw concrete ceilings, with pink carpets and Hollywood-style mirrors. You can listen to playlists created by Caroline de Maigret, the French model and music producer, who is also the artistic director of the hotel, on OJAS speakers. There’s a playlist called “Boogie Nights” for when you’re getting ready to go out, with music by Prince and Grace Jones, and another called (naturally) “the French Connection,” dedicated to French music with songs by Jacqueline Taïeb and La Femme. Even little things nod to music, like light switches meant to look like vintage amplifiers.

Slide into a red velvet booth for dinner by the French chef Valentin Raffali at the hotel’s evocative restaurant, which has a wall of vinyl records, including those that belonged to Bus Palladium’s founder, James Arch. Sip a cocktail at the bar before heading to the club, where you can dance until the wee hours beneath a disco ball. The hotel, part of the Chapitre Six collection of French hotels, has prices from around €490, or about $550, a night.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: What’s Riding on Anthropic’s Market Debut? Nearly Everything.
item.description:
When Anthropic goes public as soon as next month, its initial offering will be more than just a coming-out party for the artificial intelligence company. It will also be a litmus test for the economy, with trillions of dollars at stake.

Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, is a tent pole of the A.I. industry. Valued in the private markets at nearly $1 trillion and backed by more than $130 billion in funding, it could raise $100 billion in its offering and promptly become one of the world’s biggest public companies. But the stakes are even higher than that.

Anthropic and OpenAI, its chief rival, sit atop a pyramid of business partners and suppliers — infrastructure providers, chipmakers, energy companies and A.I. start-ups — that have all spent heavily over the last four years because they believe demand for A.I. products will keep growing.

Anthropic’s listing will provide the first in-depth look at the health of a key business underlying the A.I. boom — and will be a test of its durability. Is there unending appetite for A.I. services to justify the spending on chips, data centers and other infrastructure? Or will Anthropic’s performance show that there are limits?

“For the market, it’s a bellwether,” said Umesh Padval, an investor at Seligman Ventures, who has worked in tech for nearly 40 years.

If Anthropic disappoints in its public debut, that could hurt investor confidence and cascade into a wider market sell-off, casting doubts on how much longer the A.I. boom can go. A successful offering could lift the market and pave the way for more A.I. companies to go public.

Stock markets are already on edge, with technology stocks broadly falling this month, led by a sell-off in the companies that design and produce the computer chips that power A.I. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is in a bear market, defined as a decline of 20 percent or more from a recent high and a sign of significant investor angst, after falling 26 percent from its June peak.

Over the last couple of weeks, Microsoft canceled a deal with Nscale, a provider of data centers. A report from the research firm Gartner predicted that 80 percent of “neoclouds,” the companies that provide data and computing power for A.I. firms, could be forced out of business. And Ken Griffin, the billionaire owner of the hedge fund Citadel, said A.I. investors were “almost certainly” in a bubble.

Those negative signals have added to fears about the huge piles of money being spent on A.I. infrastructure. Amazon, Meta, Google and Microsoft have said they plan to spend at least $740 billion on A.I. infrastructure, including data centers, this year. Private market investors have poured $1.1 trillion into Anthropic, OpenAI and other A.I. companies since 2022, according to PitchBook, which tracks investments.

As spending and investment have risen in private markets, public investments have grown, too, increasing the stock market’s reliance on the performance of the A.I. industry. The top 10 stocks in the S&P 500 are worth more than $1 trillion together, with eight of them being tech companies. Combined, the top 10 account for over 40 percent of the index, up from less than 20 percent a decade ago.

When Anthropic is added to the index, it is likely to displace either Berkshire Hathaway or Eli Lilly, the only non-tech companies with valuations above $1 trillion, from the top 10.

“There is a lot riding on this one,” said Brad Gastwirth, the global head of research and market intelligence at Circular Technology, a supply chain services firm. “If it goes bad, it’s going to bring down the market.”

This month, Anthropic gathered investors at its San Francisco headquarters to present its financial performance and growth plans. By most measures, its numbers were astounding. The company’s revenue hit $16.8 billion in the third quarter, up 45 percent from the prior quarter. But investors compared that with even faster growth of 141 percent in the second quarter.

How Anthropic explains that slowdown will be important. If it was because the company lost market share to OpenAI or companies using cheaper open-source A.I. models — the technology that powers chatbots and other tools that generate videos, text and computer code — that means the overall demand for A.I. services remains healthy. If Anthropic’s growth slowed because the entire market saw less demand for A.I. products, the reaction could be more dramatic.

Anthropic declined to comment. (The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

For the past year, Anthropic has been Silicon Valley’s hottest company, thanks partly to Claude Code, the service that transformed how software engineers write code. The company’s revenue soared, causing private market investors to drive up its valuation to $965 billion, topping OpenAI.

To meet the demand for its A.I. products, Anthropic struck deals worth hundreds of billions to lease computing power from Google, Amazon and Microsoft. It has also spent on chips from Nvidia and data centers from Nscale and others. The companies serving Anthropic are, in turn, shelling out money to their suppliers.

But over the summer, some Anthropic customers concluded they were spending too much on “tokens,” or units of data processed and generated by A.I. systems. They sought cheaper options. Meta, one of Anthropic’s largest customers, projected this year that it would spend as much as $10 billion a year on the company’s technology, but pulled back as it switched to other A.I. models.

Stocks of some A.I. companies that went public this year have wilted. Shares of Cerebras, a Silicon Valley maker of A.I. chips, have fallen roughly 40 percent from their offering price in May. Shares of Accelevation, an A.I. infrastructure company, are trading about a third lower than their $18 offering price in September. Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which went public in June, has also fallen far from its peak, though it remains roughly 9 percent above its offering price.

Against this backdrop, the market for initial public offerings has slowed. Holtec, which provides nuclear energy to the A.I. sector, withdrew its listing last month. SB Energy, a data center company controlled by SoftBank, one of OpenAI’s biggest backers, and Aggreko, a power company that works with data centers, have delayed their plans to go public.

A.I. infrastructure is a “dominant theme” of the I.P.O. market this year, said Matthew Kennedy, a senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, which tracks public listings. “It’s also been among the hardest hit by the sell-off these past few weeks.”

Bankers have warned companies that they may not get the valuations they were contemplating just two months ago. In an earnings call this month, David Solomon, the chief executive of Goldman Sachs, said that while the market for public offerings was “wide open,” companies seeking valuations close to those discussed this summer might choose to wait.

“Things got a little bit softer in September,” he said.

Anthropic’s revenue numbers have added to the doubts. The company had been expected to go public at a valuation as high as $2 trillion. But after seeing the slowing growth and the market doldrums, some investors have started discussing a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $1.7 trillion, according to one person with knowledge of the matter.

A.I. executives have been trying to provide reassurance. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, which supplies chips to the A.I. sector, saw “no ceiling” to its profits, its chief executive, C.C. Wei, said this month.

Late last week, amid growing concerns about A.I. spending, the markets fell further. The tech-heavy Nasdaq experienced its largest drop since June.

Sri Muppidi contributed reporting from San Francisco, and Joe Rennison from New York.
